headline: Microsoft, maker of the software inside the PC, goes public
text: Microsoft sold shares to the public for the first time on 13 March at 21 dollars, raising 61 million dollars; they closed the first day at about 28 dollars. Founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, it writes MS-DOS, the operating system of the IBM PC and its many copies, and released Windows 1.0 in November 1985. Sales for the year to June 1986 are about 198 million dollars.
imageCaption: Bill Gates with a Tandy 2000 running Windows 1.0, 1984

headline: Berkshire's net worth jumped 48% in 1985
text: Buffett's letter of 4 March reports that net worth rose 613.6 million dollars, or 48.2%, in 1985, to 1,643.71 dollars a share. Right after year end Berkshire bought Scott Fetzer of Cleveland, maker of World Book encyclopedias and Kirby vacuum cleaners, for about 320 million dollars, and its Capital Cities/ABC stake is now in place. 'Neither will be seen again in my lifetime,' Buffett says of Halley's Comet and the percentage gain.
imageCaption: Downtown Omaha, Nebraska, where Berkshire Hathaway has its headquarters

headline: Bank of Japan cuts rates again; bank shares jump
text: The Bank of Japan cut its discount rate to 4.0% on 10 March, its second cut this year after a reduction from 5.0% to 4.5% on 30 January, to support an economy hurt by the strong yen. Cheaper money lowers what banks pay for funds and lifts the value of their shareholdings. IBJ shares rose 45% in March.
imageCaption: The Bank of Japan head office, Tokyo

headline: Chernobyl: a Soviet reactor explodes and a radioactive cloud drifts over Europe
text: In the early hours of 26 April reactor number four of the Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine exploded and burned. The Soviet Union said nothing until 28 April, after radiation alarms went off at a Swedish plant more than 1,000 kilometres away; that evening Moscow admitted "an accident" with "one of the nuclear reactors damaged". The 53,000 people of the plant workers' town, Pripyat, were taken away by bus on 27 April, and a 10-kilometre zone around the plant was emptied. Two workers are known to have died in the explosion; how many are sick from radiation, and how far the fallout reaches, is not yet known.
imageCaption: The destroyed reactor building at Chernobyl, Ukraine, April 1986

headline: After Chernobyl: the zone widens to 30 kilometres, Europe tests its milk and vegetables
text: Ten days after the explosion the evacuation zone around Chernobyl was widened to 30 kilometres, taking some 68,000 more people from their homes; in Kiev the May Day parade went ahead, shortened to under two hours. Across Europe governments measured the fallout and told people what not to eat and drink, from fresh vegetables to milk, with rules differing from one border to the next. Twenty-eight of the plant workers and firemen have died of radiation sickness in the weeks since the fire.
imageCaption: Chernobyl seen from the SPOT-1 satellite, 1 May 1986
imageCredit: Images SPOT acquises dans le cadre du programme Spot World Heritage du CNES

headline: BMW jumps 40% as foreign money returns
text: After a weak spring, German shares rose again in August on orders from abroad; foreign investors are betting on a further rise of the mark and on lower interest rates, and by the end of the month the market was close to its April record. BMW, which raised new capital in July with a rights issue, rose fastest. Its new 7 Series luxury saloon has been in production since June.

headline: Rising bond yields send shares down 9 percent
text: Shares fell sharply in September as long-term interest rates rose: yields on Treasury bonds climbed as much as 0.6 percentage point in a few weeks, although the Federal Reserve had cut its discount rate in August. Germany and Japan did not follow the American rate cut, raising worries about the dollar. The S&P 500 lost 9% in the month to 231.32, its worst month since March 1980.
imageCaption: President Reagan leads a Cabinet meeting at the White House, 11 September 1986

headline: Schlumberger ousts its chairman as the oil slump bites
text: On 2 October Schlumberger's board removed chairman Michel Vaillaud after about a year and elected Euan Baird, 49, as chairman, president and chief executive, the first non-Frenchman to run the company. First-half profit fell to 203 million dollars from 516 million. Oilfield services bring 65 percent of revenue, and 86 percent of 1985 profit came from the US and Canadian oilfields, where drilling has collapsed.
imageCaption: The P-51 offshore oil platform, Brazil

headline: Schweizerhalle: fire at a Sandoz warehouse poisons the Rhine
text: In the early hours of 1 November a fire destroyed a Sandoz warehouse at Schweizerhalle near Basel holding about 1,350 tonnes of pesticides and other farm chemicals. Firefighting water carried the chemicals into the Rhine, turning it red and killing fish and eels from Switzerland through West Germany to the Netherlands; acrid smoke drifted over Basel. The cause of the fire is not known.
imageCaption: Clean-up after the fire at the Sandoz warehouse in Schweizerhalle near Basel, November 1986
